clue.text: Put paid to beauty contest winner?

definitions.meaning: to put paid to someone's hopes is to ruin them
an informal noun for a very good-looking person, the sort who might win such a contest

explanation.surface: Someone ended a pageant champion's reign.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: the slang verb meaning to wreck someone's chances, and the slang noun for an attractive person.

clue.text: Servicemen ready with marine markers, we hear

parts.note: ready (or readies) is British slang for cash, as is dough

indicators.note: says that the floats' name is to be taken by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: buoys are floats marking channels or hazards at sea

explanation.surface: Troops stand prepared alongside navigation floats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' applies only to the second piece: the floats are said, then spelt as a word for lads.
explanation.definitionFit: A historical nickname for American infantrymen, especially in the First World War.

clue.text: Student of the sun, pinning down carbon and hydrogen

indicators.note: the sun word holds the two element symbols fast inside it, as a pin traps something

parts.note: solar is the adjective for things relating to the sun
C is the chemical symbol for carbon
H is the chemical symbol for hydrogen

explanation.surface: An astronomy student analyses the sun's chemistry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pinning down' puts CH inside SOLAR, after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: A learned person or one studying, so a synonym for a student in the broad sense.

clue.text: Soprano with endlessly vocal jazz fans carrying 29 types of headwear

indicators.note: says the word for vocal loses its final letter

parts.note: loud describes a vocal, outspoken person

indicators.note: the fans hold the other piece inside them, as if carrying it

parts.note: cats is old jazz slang for its enthusiasts
the number points to the across entry whose H-shaped goals are written here as the letters HH

explanation.surface: A singer accompanies noisy jazz fans who are carrying gear for some sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' drops D; 'carrying' wraps the jazz fans round the 29 letters. Throughout this puzzle 29 gives HH, the two H-shaped sets of goals at each end of the pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: These broad-brimmed felt hats, one side often turned up, are a kind of headgear, famously Australian army issue.

clue.text: March and rally heading off wrongly, prompting tears

indicators.note: the combined letters are put together wrongly, in a new order
the first letter of rally, its head, is removed

explanation.surface: A protest march and rally go badly awry and end in tears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading off' leaves ALLY; 'wrongly' rearranges MARCH plus ALLY.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective relates to weeping and the glands that produce it, so it fits something causing crying.

clue.text: Usual changes, not special, but very necessary for part of mouth

indicators.note: means the remaining letters undergo changes of order
means the letter for special is left out of the first word

explanation.surface: Speech habits change, yet some feature of the mouth remains essential.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes S from USUAL; 'changes' reorders what is left together with V, the V being 'necessary' for the result.
explanation.definitionFit: The small fleshy lobe hanging at the back of the soft palate is a component of the oral cavity.

clue.text: Wells, say, including one with 29 fish — soles of extended size

indicators.note: the initials take the numeral inside them

parts.note: H. G. Wells, the novelist, gives his initials HG
I is the Roman numeral for one
the number points to the across entry whose H-shaped goals are written here as the letters HH
eels are long snake-like fish

explanation.surface: The novelist Wells, with a cross-reference and some fish, in a jumble of nouns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wells, say' means any Wells will do: here the novelist H. G. Wells, by his initials. 'including' wraps them round the numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Raised footwear adds height, so its soles are cryptically ones of greater dimension.

clue.text: 30s style rated 'dreadful' by company

indicators.note: something dreadful is in a bad state, so the letters are put into disorder

explanation.surface: A firm judged an interwar design trend to be awful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dreadful' rearranges RATED into ARTDE.
explanation.definitionFit: The geometric decorative movement flourished in the 1920s and 1930s, so it is a style of that era.

clue.text: Goes climbing, securing line — try dropping off?

indicators.note: the reversed word grips the line letter inside it, like a climber's rope
in a down entry, climbing means the word is written upwards, back to front

parts.note: goes is a euphemism for urinates, which is pees

explanation.surface: A climber goes up, fixing a rope, and tries not to fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climbing' turns PEES into SEEP; 'securing' holds L inside to give S-L-EEP. 'dropping off' sounds like a fall but means nodding off.
explanation.definitionFit: Dropping off means falling asleep, so 'try dropping off' is a command to doze.

clue.text: Close call, nothing less

indicators.note: means the zero letter is taken away from the call word

parts.note: to shout is to call out loudly
O is the figure for nothing, zero

explanation.surface: A near thing, minus nothing at all.
explanation.definitionFit: To close a door is to make it fast, a simple verb synonym.

clue.text: 29 in universities heading for Humanities, I suppose

indicators.note: the cross-reference letters sit in the middle of the pair of university abbreviations

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for university, doubled for the plural
the number points to the across entry whose H-shaped goals are written here as the letters HH

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Sporting facilities at universities lead the way for the arts, one presumes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts HH between the two Us; 'heading for' takes H from Humanities.
explanation.definitionFit: A grudging spoken affirmative, equivalent to saying yes, that's probably so.

clue.text: Royal attendants about to receive English vegetable

indicators.note: the attendants surround the verb, going about it

parts.note: a court is the body of courtiers around a monarch
to get is to receive

explanation.surface: Courtiers are about to be handed an English vegetable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to receive' looks like 'on the point of receiving', but 'about' is the container and 'to receive' gives GET.
explanation.definitionFit: The courgette, the zucchini to Americans, is a summer squash eaten as a vegetable.

clue.text: Army turned about, having seized large weapon-carrier

indicators.note: the combined letters grab the size letter and hold it inside

parts.note: a host is an army, as in the heavenly host

indicators.note: means the two letters for about are turned round

parts.note: re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: A retreating army grabs a big gun-case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' applies only to 'about', not the army; 'having seized' puts the size letter after the first two letters of the combined word.
explanation.definitionFit: A leather case worn at the hip or shoulder carries a pistol, so it is a gun-carrier.

clue.text: Pile of rubbish apparently includes 29, in the main

indicators.note: the abbreviation wraps around everything else, its two letters at either end

parts.note: app. is a dictionary abbreviation for apparently, shortened here to AP

indicators.note: the cross-reference letters go in the word for the main

parts.note: the main is a poetic term for the open sea
the number points to the across entry whose H-shaped goals are written here as the letters HH

explanation.surface: Junk seemingly contains sports goals and ends up out at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'apparently' reads as a hedge on the definition but is the dictionary abbreviation app., cut to two letters; 'includes' makes it the outer shell, with 'in' working inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A mound of cinders and household refuse, so a dump or pile of waste.

clue.text: Maroon was released by traveller afloat?

indicators.note: the letters are set free from their order and recombined

explanation.surface: A castaway was freed by a passing sailor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maroon' looks like the castaway's plight but is fodder, with 'was'; 'released' rearranges the eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A female rower travels on water, a cryptic description of someone propelling a boat.

clue.text: Succeed with energy and light, enthralling Newton

indicators.note: the word with holds the unit symbol inside it, captivating it

parts.note: N is the symbol for the newton, the unit of force
E is the symbol for energy in physics
day means daylight, light

explanation.surface: Physics triumphs with energy and light, captivating the great Newton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enthralling' puts N inside WITH to give WINTH.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom meaning to prevail or come out on top, so to succeed.

clue.text: Supplier of information: green pond's third to be circled by amphibian

indicators.note: the amphibian surrounds the colour and the letter

parts.note: a newt is a small amphibian
sage is a grey-green colour

indicators.note: picks out the third letter of the pond word

explanation.surface: A newt circling a green pond seems to know what is going on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'green' looks like the colour of the pond but is a separate piece; 'third' picks one letter of pond's, and 'to be circled by' sets both inside the amphibian.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop or trader selling newspapers and magazines supplies the news, hence information.

clue.text: Manage to retreat, getting hard time

indicators.note: retreating goes backwards, so the word is written back to front

parts.note: to cope is to manage
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Coping by withdrawing makes for a tough period.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to retreat' reverses COPE into EPOC.
explanation.definitionFit: An era or period of history, so a span of time.

clue.text: Thick, i.e. daft, to carry 29 in travel by road

indicators.note: the scrambled letters hold the cross-reference letters within them
silly or crazy, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: the number points to the across entry whose H-shaped goals are written here as the letters HH

explanation.surface: A dim person has to lug sporting equipment on a road trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thick, i.e.' looks like a dictionary gloss but is the anagram fodder; 'daft' rearranges it and 'to carry' holds the 29 letters inside after its fourth letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Thumbing lifts from passing drivers is a way of journeying along roads.

clue.text: Half-hearted attempt to start up a new form of transport

indicators.note: the doubled middle of the word, its heart, is halved, losing one of its two letters

parts.note: to seed something is to try to get it started, as with a fund or a crop

explanation.surface: A feeble effort to launch a novel means of transport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-hearted' halves the double E at the centre of SEED, leaving SED.
explanation.definitionFit: A saloon car, in American usage, or the older sedan chair carried on poles: both are ways of getting about.

clue.text: Vigorous water sport held around river

indicators.note: the sport word is held around the river letter

parts.note: diving is an aquatic sport

explanation.surface: A water sport is staged near a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Driving rain or a driving force is forceful and energetic, so the adjective means powerful.

clue.text: Port frequently given a poor rating?

parts.note: the lowest is the poorest possible rating
oft is an old word for often

explanation.surface: Something is often given low marks.
explanation.walkthrough: LOWESTOFT is a fishing port in Suffolk, England's most easterly town. Read the clue as 'rated lowest oft'.
explanation.definitionFit: A coastal town with a harbour on the North Sea, so a port by name.

clue.text: Soldiers, if leading reserve, will get opening

parts.note: OR stands for Other Ranks, ordinary soldiers
ice means reserve, a cool, distant manner

explanation.surface: Troops will find a way forward if they lead the reserves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reserve' sounds military but means coolness of manner, ICE.
explanation.definitionFit: A hole or aperture, so a synonym for an opening.

clue.text: Male I leave, around 29 — what does it matter?

parts.note: he is the male pronoun

indicators.note: the departure word sits around the cross-reference letters

parts.note: to go is to leave
the number points to the across entry whose H-shaped goals are written here as the letters HH

explanation.surface: A man walks off past the goals with a shrug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leave' is a verb here, not part of 'I leave' as a sentence: the I stands alone and 'around' wraps the leaving word round the 29 letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation of weary resignation, meaning roughly oh well, never mind.

clue.text: No repeat appearance for milliner one dislikes

indicators.note: the letter appearing twice in a row is denied its second appearance

parts.note: a hatter makes hats, as a milliner does

explanation.surface: A milliner who will never be booked again is resented.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No repeat appearance for' drops one of the doubled Ts in HATTER.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who loathes something is a person who dislikes it.

clue.text: Cheers success in support of old NZ university

indicators.note: in a down entry, the following pieces are written below the old letter, supporting it

parts.note: ta is British informal for thanks, like cheers
to make a go of it is to succeed, so a go is a success

explanation.surface: Applause for a triumph backing an old New Zealand university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheers' means thanks here, TA, not applause.
explanation.definitionFit: Otago University in Dunedin is the oldest university in New Zealand.

clue.text: Article's effusiveness about one in pain

parts.note: an is the indefinite article

indicators.note: the gushing word goes about the numeral

parts.note: gush is effusive, over-the-top talk
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A gushing article about someone suffering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts I inside GUSH to give GUISH.
explanation.definitionFit: Severe mental or physical suffering, so a near synonym for pain.

clue.text: Vessel almost capsized in capture

indicators.note: a capsized boat is upside down, so in a down entry the letters run upwards
the boat word loses its last letter

parts.note: a barge is a flat-bottomed boat

explanation.surface: A boat nearly overturned while being seized.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' leaves BARG; 'capsized' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: To seize or snatch something is to capture it.

clue.text: Awful expression of annoyance creeping into tense employment arrangement

parts.note: T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

indicators.note: the curse slips inside the other letters

parts.note: hire is the arrangement by which one takes someone on, or rents something
drat is a mild curse

explanation.surface: Muttered complaints spread through a strained workplace deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tense' is an adjective in the surface but a grammar term here; 'creeping into' slips the curse inside the word for employment, after its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something of poor quality, a long way below the best, is dreadful.

clue.text: Most of all, I attempt to overlook daughter's justification

indicators.note: the word all loses one letter, its last

parts.note: taken as written before the cut

indicators.note: the daughter letter is overlooked, left out of the attempt word

parts.note: a bid is an attempt

explanation.surface: Mostly, a father tries to ignore his daughter's excuse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most of' cuts ALL to AL; 'to overlook' drops D from BID, leaving BI.
explanation.definitionFit: A claim of having been elsewhere excuses a suspect, so it is a defence or excuse.

clue.text: Mat, according to online comments, is a feature of sport

parts.note: a rug is a floor mat
by means according to, as in by the rules
posts are comments on internet forums

explanation.surface: Internet commenters say a mat is part of sport.
explanation.definitionFit: The H-shaped goals at each end of a rugby pitch are a fixture of that game.

clue.text: Supports keeping half back for gala

indicators.note: only the back half of the word is turned round

parts.note: feet support the body

explanation.surface: Posts hold a rugby half back in place at a festive event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half back' reverses the last two letters of FEET, ET, to TE; a half back is also a rugby position, fitting the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A fair or festive outdoor event, often for charity, is a gala.
